title: A Device-Lending Program: Article and Fact Sheet
description: Use an article, fact sheet, and opposing comments to distinguish measured access outcomes from unsupported academic claims.
subject: rla
author: Studo
reviewNotes: Mixed-source Arguments practice reviewed for source comparison, evidence quality, one-best-answer logic, and ER transfer.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by BOTH the article and the fact sheet?

options.text: The pilot caused borrowers' grades to rise.
options.whyWrong: Both formats explicitly lack grade comparison data.

options.text: The program reached many students who reported limited computer access, and most surveyed borrowers said home schoolwork became easier.
Every student in the district needs a district-owned laptop.
options.whyWrong: Only borrowers and their prior access are described; need across all students is not measured.

options.text: Repair problems were too severe for any expansion.
options.whyWrong: Repairs occurred, but the sources do not establish that the rate makes expansion unworkable.

explanation.whyCorrect: This conclusion combines two directly reported findings without claiming an unmeasured academic outcome.
explanation.quickTip: When formats overlap, synthesize only the outcomes both can support.

questions.prompt: What error does Moore make with the 82 percent survey result?

options.text: She treats a self-reported improvement in ease of doing schoolwork as proof that grades increased.
She understates the percentage of borrowers with limited access.
options.whyWrong: Her argument centers on the 82 percent survey, not the 71 percent access figure.

options.text: She claims no students borrowed laptops.
She ignores the repair data and therefore proves repairs never occurred.
options.whyWrong: Ignoring repair data is incomplete, but it does not create the specific grade-causation error.

explanation.whyCorrect: The survey measures perceived ease, while grades are a different outcome that the pilot did not compare.
explanation.quickTip: Do not substitute a nearby outcome for the one named in the claim.

questions.prompt: Why is Bell's argument better calibrated to the evidence than Moore's?

options.text: Bell rejects all expansion until perfect evidence exists.
options.whyWrong: He supports expanding the loan pool while adding measures.

options.text: Bell distinguishes the access claim the pilot supports from the grade claim it has not measured.
Bell assumes repair costs are zero.
options.whyWrong: He does not make that claim.

options.text: Bell relies only on his personal opinion.
options.whyWrong: He cites the access and borrower-survey evidence and proposes new measures.

explanation.whyCorrect: He matches each conclusion to what the pilot actually measured and identifies what new data would be needed for a stronger claim.
explanation.quickTip: Strong arguments separate supported conclusions from questions that remain open.

questions.prompt: What does the fact-sheet format contribute that is especially useful for evaluating the board comments?

options.text: It clearly separates measured results from outcomes the pilot did not measure.
It proves every number in the news article is false.
options.whyWrong: The two formats are consistent on the main figures.

options.text: It gives emotional stories about individual borrowers.
options.whyWrong: The fact sheet is concise and numerical rather than anecdotal.

options.text: It recommends buying laptops for every student.
options.whyWrong: The fact sheet reports pilot scope and limits; it does not make that policy recommendation.

explanation.whyCorrect: The explicit “did not measure” bullets make it easier to detect when a speaker crosses from evidence into an unsupported outcome claim.
explanation.quickTip: Different formats can make limitations as important as findings easier to see.

questions.prompt: Which new evidence would most directly test Moore's claim about grades?

options.text: A larger survey asking whether laptops look modern.
Repair totals from another semester.
options.whyWrong: Repair data matter to feasibility, not academic performance.

options.text: Course-grade or assignment-completion comparisons over time between similar students with and without reliable computer access through the program.
A list of websites students visit on school devices.
options.whyWrong: Browsing data alone would not establish whether grades improve.

explanation.whyCorrect: This measures the academic outcomes Moore claims and creates a comparison that can help separate program access from other influences.
explanation.quickTip: Add evidence that directly measures the missing outcome.

questions.prompt: Which statement best compares the two board comments?

options.text: Both agree the pilot proves higher grades, but Bell wants fewer devices.
options.whyWrong: Bell explicitly says the grade effect is not proven.

options.text: Moore treats access/ease evidence as sufficient for an academic-performance claim, while Bell supports the access conclusion and calls for new evidence before making the stronger grade claim.
Moore focuses on repairs, while Bell focuses only on late returns.
options.whyWrong: Their main disagreement is about what the pilot proves academically.

options.text: Both reject the device-lending program.
options.whyWrong: Both support some form of expansion.

explanation.whyCorrect: This comparison identifies the exact difference in evidentiary standards rather than exaggerating their policy disagreement.
explanation.quickTip: Compare what each writer thinks the evidence is sufficient to establish.

curriculum.learningObjective: Evaluate claims, evidence, reasoning, and multiple sources under GED-style conditions.
